speaker: Doctor
text: I see you are experiencing jaundice, pruritus, weight loss, pale stools, and dark urine. To help me narrow down the cause, can you tell me if you have been experiencing any abdominal pain, fever, or nausea?

text: 72-year-old male. The patient has experienced gradual yellow discoloration of the skin and generalized pruritus over the past 2 weeks. He also reports a decreased appetite and a weight loss of 6.3 kg (14 lb). The patient’s stool has been pale, and his urine is very dark. Three years ago, he had an episode of acute upper abdominal pain, which was managed with IV fluids, NSAIDs, and dietary modification. speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that history. To help me differentiate between a malignant obstruction and other causes, have you noticed any specific changes in your abdominal pain pattern, or do you have a history of gallstones? I would also like to check for a palpable gallbladder, so please take a deep breath in while I press on the right upper quadrant of your abdomen.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your significant smoking history and risk factors, I need to check for signs of pancreatic or biliary malignancy. REQUEST TEST: Abdominal_CT_Scan

speaker: Doctor
text: The CT scan results indicate normal readings, which is unexpected given the obstructive symptoms. I need to visualize the biliary tree directly to rule out a small stone or stricture not seen on CT. REQUEST TEST: MRCP

speaker: Doctor
text: The MRCP also shows normal readings, which effectively rules out structural obstructions like stones or tumors in the bile ducts. Given the negative imaging and your history, we must consider intrahepatic causes such as primary sclerosing cholangitis or drug-induced liver injury. Do you have a history of inflammatory bowel disease, or are you currently taking any new medications or supplements?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Episode of acute upper abdominal pain treated three years ago. History of long-term alcohol consumption and smoking. Social history: Stopped alcohol consumption three years ago; 50-year history of smoking a pack of cigarettes daily.

speaker: Doctor
text: You have confirmed no history of inflammatory bowel disease or new medications, which makes primary sclerosing cholangitis and drug-induced liver injury less likely. Given the classic presentation of painless jaundice, weight loss, and a significant smoking history in an elderly male, this is highly suspicious for pancreatic head adenocarcinoma, which may have been missed on initial CT if the lesion was small or isodense. DIAGNOSIS READY: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma
